content:
There is, of course, no specific "auto replay" feature in Thunderbird, though the same thing can be done using a combination of Message Filters and Templates. If you are absolutely sure that there are no filters or templates, then I don't think it can have come from Thunderbird and must be being generated on the server side.

A test for this could be to move the msgFilterRules.dat and TEMPLATES folder files out of your profile (while Thunderbird is closed.) TEMPLATES will be regenerated, and you can put the filter rules file back after the test.

The only other thing I can think of is that a reply wound up in the local Outbox folder, where they normally go when created while offline, with the intention of being sent later when you're back online, and that it's somehow stuck there. If you don't find it there, I think you've eliminated all local possibilities.

Such 'auto-replys' are sometimes called 'out-of-office' messages on web mail settings.

Anti-virus software can cause many problems in Thunderbird. I believe that at least some of your symptoms can be caused by anti-virus software. The common recommendation on the forum is not to use any anti-virus software other than what Microsoft includes in Windows. If one insists on using third-party anti-virus software, one should create an exception for Thunderbird in it and read the information here: https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/security-panel-settings-in-thunderbird

If McAfee is causing some problems, I do not know why they starting happening only recently. Maybe the software was updated.

You do seem to have problems other than those that are caused by anti-virus software. But removing Thunderbird and re-installing rarely fixes anything.

In your place, I would first try Thunderbird in troubleshooting mode (under the "Help" menu) and see if the problems persist or which ones persist.

If some problems persist, I would then start Windows in safe mode with netorking turned on. Some people report that this requires an Ethernet connnection because wi-fi does not work in safe mode. If you cannot do that, then disable McAfee and test Thunderbird again. I do not know if you must re-start Windows after disabling McAfee.

If you really want to remove Thunderbird, you can delete the app, which is stored separately from your profile, and you won't lose data. But back up your profile first because we all make mistakes.

content:
It could be that your mail provider rightly or wrongly considers this to be spam and is moving it to the Spam folder before you ever download it. You could verify this by checking web mail before fetching to Thunderbird. The provider may also have its own filtering or whitelisting features.

As a test you could disable all Thunderbird spam controls and observer what happens with this particular contact. If it still ends up in Spam, that would support the above theory.

It's possible that Thunderbird's Adaptive Filtering's database is corrupt. You can reset it at <Settings | Privacy & Security | Junk | Reset Training Data>. This would require you to train it all over again from scratch, so maybe do this as a last resort.

The porn spam will be hard to control unless there is a specific common trait they all share. Possibly a filter with a list of naughty words in the Subject might work, but I bet a lot would slip through. Spammers have tricks to get around filtering on literal criteria. The Adaptive controls are the most effective tool for that, though of course, it can never be 100%

My observation is that spam comes in waves. It will ramp up for a while, hit a peak, then fade away until the next campaign. I deal with it the best I can with the available tools and live with what's left.

Spamassassin depends on if your email provider uses it and if you trust its decisions. If it doesn't offer that service, turning it on in Thunderbird will do nothing, though it won't hurt anything, either. I guess it can't hurt to try.
